content.body: Searching a 2D matrix efficiently is a common challenge. Today, we'll learn how to find a target value in a sorted 2D matrix without checking every single cell. This technique combines what you know about arrays with a clever lookup strategy.
content.title: Introduction

content.body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
1. Explain why a naive search through every cell is inefficient.
2. Apply the concept of treating a 2D matrix as a single sorted list.
3. Implement an efficient search using a single pass with a lookup structure.
4. Determine what to store as keys and values in your lookup.
5. Decide when to check the lookup versus when to add to it.
content.title: What you'll learn
Try it
content.prompt: Find the number 5 in this small 2x2 matrix. What cell is it in?
content.successMessage: Great! You found 5 at row 1, column 0 (or index [1][0]).

content.title: Try a bigger matrix
content.prompt: Now find 20 in this 3x3 matrix. Which cell contains it?
content.successMessage: Well done! You checked several cells and noticed 20 isn't here. You might have scanned row by row.

content.title: One more
content.prompt: Find 34 in this 4x4 matrix. How many cells did you check?
content.successMessage: Excellent! You likely checked multiple rows and columns. With 16 cells, checking each one starts to feel tedious.

content.body: What you just did was a linear search: you looked at cells one by one, either row-by-row or column-by-column. For a small matrix, this works, but it doesn't scale well.
content.title: What you did

content.body: Imagine a matrix with 10,000 rows and 10,000 columns—that's 100 million cells! Checking each cell individually would be extremely slow. We need a smarter method that avoids unnecessary checks. Can't figure it out? Click Show me on the next step.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: The secret is to remember what we have already seen. Instead of re-scanning cells, we can use a lookup structure (like an object or Map) to track values and their positions. This way, we check each cell only once and instantly know if we've found our target.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Think of it like a notebook where we write down every number we see and its location. Before checking a new cell, we look in our notebook to see if we've already found the number we need.

content.body: We'll treat the 2D matrix as if it were a single sorted list. We'll use a single pass through the matrix, storing each value and its position in a lookup. For each cell, we check if the complement (target - current value) is already in our lookup. If it is, we've found our pair. If not, we add the current value to the lookup.
content.title: The approach
content.illustratedExample:
Let's walk through a 2x3 matrix [[2, 7, 11], [15, 19, 23]] with target 26.
1. Check 2 at [0,0] → need 24? Not in lookup. Add 2.
2. Check 7 at [0,1] → need 19? Not in lookup. Add 7.
3. Check 11 at [0,2] → need 15? Not in lookup. Add 11.
4. Check 15 at [1,0] → need 11? Yes! 11 is in lookup at [0,2]. Found pair: [0,2] and [1,0].

content.body:
Here's our plan:
1. Create an empty lookup (object or Map).
2. Loop through each row in the matrix.
3. For each cell in the row:
   a. Calculate the complement (target - current value).
   b. Check if the complement exists in the lookup.
   c. If yes, return the positions of complement and current cell.
   d. If no, add the current value and its position to the lookup.
4. If loop finishes, target not found.
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Set up the function and lookup
steps.instruction: Create a function called searchMatrix that takes a matrix and target. Initialize an empty object called seen to act as our lookup.
steps.hint: Remember: the lookup will store values as keys and their [row, col] positions as values.
steps.expectedOutcome: Function defined with empty lookup object.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've set up the foundation.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you create an empty object inside the function.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's start simple: define the function and create an empty object called 'seen'.

steps.title: Loop through rows
steps.instruction: Add a loop to iterate through each row of the matrix using a for loop.
steps.hint: Use for (let row = 0; row < matrix.length; row++) to go through each row.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! Now we can access each row.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost. Make sure your loop goes from 0 to matrix.length.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try: for (let row = 0; row < matrix.length; row++) { }

steps.title: Loop through columns
steps.instruction: Inside the row loop, add another loop to iterate through each column in the current row.
steps.hint: Use for (let col = 0; col < matrix[row].length; col++) to go through each column.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! Now we can access each cell.
steps.feedbackPartial: Close. The inner loop should use matrix[row].length.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try: for (let col = 0; col < matrix[row].length; col++) { }

steps.title: Check the lookup
steps.instruction: Inside the column loop, get the current cell's value. Calculate the complement (target - value). Check if the complement exists in seen. If it does, return the positions.
steps.hint: Use if (complement in seen) to check. Return [seen[complement], [row, col]] if found.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Well done! You're checking our notebook before adding new entries.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start. Remember to calculate complement and check if it's in 'seen'.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try: const value = matrix[row][col]; const complement = target - value; if (complement in seen) return [seen[complement], [row, col]];

steps.title: Add to the lookup
steps.instruction: If the complement wasn't found, add the current value and its position to the seen object. After the loops, return false or null to indicate not found.
steps.hint: Use seen[value] = [row, col] to store the position. Place this after the if check.
steps.expectedOutcome: Add to lookup and final return added.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Don't forget to add the current value to 'seen' and return something at the end.
steps.feedbackWrong: Add: seen[value] = [row, col]; after the if. Then after loops: return null;

content.body: Congratulations! You've implemented an efficient search for a 2D matrix using a lookup structure. Remember: the key idea is to remember what we've already seen to avoid re-scanning. Store values as keys and their positions as values in your lookup. Always check the lookup before adding new entries. This approach transforms an O(n²) problem into O(n), making it scalable for large matrices.
